title: What Can Be Computed with Indefinite Causal Structure?
abstract: Can quantum computation become more powerful when operations do not need to follow a definite causal order? We study this question in the process matrix formalism of Oreshkov et al. (Nature Communications, 2012), which allows quantum operations to be connected without a fixed global order. In the computational model, a quantum circuit succinctly describes a process matrix, and the algorithm is given access to its generated channel, with computational cost measured by the size of the generating circuit.   We give polynomial-time algorithms in two settings. First, general process matrix computation suffices to solve every problem in $\textbf{NP}$. The valid processes used by our algorithm satisfy the purification postulate of Araújo et al. (Quantum, 2017), and their generated channels are unitary, although their generating circuits are not. Second, requiring the process matrices themselves to be pure, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for unique-sink orientation, a general problem capturing several longstanding computational problems in optimization. Our unitary generators are constructed explicitly and efficiently. Assuming that unique-sink orientation has no quantum polynomial-time algorithm, our result shows that indefinite causal order can provide computational power beyond $\textbf{BQP}$ within the process matrix formalism, even while preserving unitarity.
summary: This work explores quantum computation under an indefinite causal structure using the Process Matrix Formalism. It demonstrates that this framework allows for solving all NP problems and, under specific conditions, suggests computational power exceeding BQP. The research is significant for understanding the fundamental limits of quantum computation when causality constraints are relaxed.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether quantum computation can gain enhanced power when the sequence of operations does not need to follow a fixed, definite causal order.
main_result: It shows that general process matrix computation is sufficient to solve every problem in NP, and under certain restrictions, indefinite causal order can provide computational power beyond BQP, even while maintaining unitarity.
method: The analysis uses the Process Matrix Formalism (PMF) to model quantum operations without fixed causality, establishing computational complexity bounds by relating the structure of the generating circuits to known complexity classes.
model_or_system: The core model is the Process Matrix Formalism, which describes correlations between quantum operations. The computation is modeled by a quantum circuit generating a process matrix, with complexity measured by the circuit size.
key_observables: Computational complexity classes (NP, BQP), the process matrix itself, and the operator norm/Frobenius norm used to bound approximation errors.
important_parameters: The restriction to pure process matrices, the approximation error parameter $\eta$, and the computational cost measured by circuit size.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the purification postulate for physical processes and makes assumptions regarding the computational difficulty of unique-sink orientation (USO).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by introducing the PMF, establishing that general computation reaches NP, then restricting to pure processes to solve USO, and finally proving bounds on the difference between related unitary operations.
why_interesting: The exploration of non-causal quantum computation provides a theoretical framework for understanding potential computational advantages beyond standard quantum circuit models, which is highly relevant to the foundations of quantum information.
